title: Nothing is impossible (Luke 1:26–38)
hook: Mary asks how, and hears: with God nothing shall be impossible

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zechariah was struck silent, and Elisabeth kept her joy hidden for five months. Your line was silence can grow things. Where did you say less, and what grew? Day five hundred five.

In the sixth month of Elisabeth's pregnancy, Luke says, the same angel is sent somewhere completely different. Not the capital, not the holy place, not to a priest. To Nazareth, a village in Galilee the Old Testament never mentions. To a young woman named Mary, engaged to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. Luke doesn't tell us her age, or what she was doing when the angel came in. Cooking, maybe. Fetching water. Ordinary hours in an ordinary house. Yesterday an old priest in a golden room. Today a girl in a village nobody's heard of. And the message she's about to receive is far stranger than his.

Gabriel's greeting, in the King James Bible: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Luke says she was troubled, and turned the words over in her mind, wondering what kind of greeting this was. Then the news: she will bear a son, she'll name him Jesus, and he will be called the Son of the Highest, and his kingdom will have no end. Mary asks a question: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Notice the difference from Zechariah. He asked, how can I be sure? She asks, how will this happen? Not proof. Just how. And Gabriel answers: the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee. Then he gives her a sign she can go and see for herself: your relative Elisabeth, the one everybody called barren, is six months along. And then the line: "For with God nothing shall be impossible." In Greek, it can also be read as no word from God will be without power. God's promises don't fall to the ground. And Mary's answer: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." Then the angel leaves. Christians across the churches treasure this scene, and they honor Mary in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor her with special devotion as the Mother of God; the Hail Mary prayer opens with Gabriel's greeting. Many Protestant Christians honor her as a model of trusting faith. All of them hear a yes in her last line: be it unto me.
screen: `BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`
then, large: `WITH GOD NOTHING SHALL BE IMPOSSIBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one impossible thing to God. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that looks impossible. A relationship that seems beyond repair. An illness. A habit you can't break. Someone you love who seems unreachable. Don't pretend it's easy. Mary didn't; she asked how. Just hold the impossible thing, honestly, the way you'd hold something heavy in both hands. Then, if you can, loosen your grip a little. If you pray, you can bring it to God, and if the words fit, say Mary's line: be it unto me according to thy word. If you don't, simply hold it open, without forcing an answer. The bell holds the time.
Gabriel. The angel who told Mary that with God nothing is impossible, and that no word from him lacks power.
Your line: be it unto me. Today, when you hear yourself say that'll never happen, pause and ask Mary's question instead: how might this be? Day five hundred five.

howItsDone: Many churches celebrate the Annunciation on March 25, nine months before Christmas; Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray the Hail Mary, which begins with Gabriel's greeting, and many Christians read this passage in Advent.

fork.setup: you're Mary. an angel has told you something impossible, and given you a sign. what do you say?
options: behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.
fork.reveal: her answer is a yes: "be it unto me according to thy word." then the angel departs.

original.note: Greek: a word, a thing spoken. Luke 1:37 can be read: no word from God will be without power.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poster slogan, anything is possible.
what it means: Gabriel's answer to Mary's how: God can do what no one else can, and Elisabeth's pregnancy is the sign.
what a scholar hears: the Greek can also mean no word from God will be powerless, so it's about God's promises never failing.

notes: Audit (y2 second sample): 'six months after the temple scene' misread Luke 1:26 ('in the sixth month', of Elisabeth's pregnancy); Luke never calls Joseph a carpenter (that is Matthew 13:55), now 'of the house of David' (1:27); 'so small it's never mentioned' turned a silence into a cause; the closing stock line 'a yes that changed everything' replaced.
Luke 1:37 Greek (ouk adynatēsei para tou theou pan rhēma) alternative reading 'no word from God will be void of power'. Confirm.
Nazareth not mentioned in the Old Testament, Josephus or the Talmud: the script says only the Old Testament.
Mary's relation to Elisabeth: KJV 'cousin', Greek syngenis (kinswoman); script says 'relative'.
Differences in Marian devotion described without ranking. Catholic/Orthodox title 'Mother of God' (Theotokos). Confirm.
